name: Crucible ForgeWall MK-3 Foundry Apron Rig
description: A heavy split-bib foundry apron in charred graphite and rust-brown, the ForgeWall MK-3 is built for high-heat forge work and arc welding. The bib and skirt panels are thick aluminized carbon-ceramic felt, visibly dimpled from spatter impacts. Cross-back harness straps are reinforced webbing with quick-release buckles at the sternum. Leg panels split at the groin for mobility, held by magnetically-clasped side tabs. The collar edge is bound in heat-treated leather analog — deep brown, cracked and re-oiled repeatedly. Crucible's forge-anvil stamp is pressed into the left chest panel.
functionality: Rated to 1,100°C radiant heat for short-duration exposure. Spatter-resistant front panels shed molten metal without ignition. Quick-release sternum buckle allows rapid removal. Split-leg design accommodates full squat and kneel positions. Compatible with chrome arm augmentations — harness adjusts wide at the shoulder.
what_it_says: You work with real fire and real metal, and your gear carries every burn to prove it.
story_hooks: A ForgeWall MK-3 with a hidden interior pocket sewn into the bib lining — the original owner used it to smuggle component chips out of a restricted fab floor.
Crucible's MK-3 is known to have a batch defect in the left-panel spatter shield — one in forty units has an under-bonded ceramic layer that delaminates under sustained heat.
A veteran forge worker's apron has forty-seven spatter impacts catalogued in a personal log stitched into the reverse — one for every serious accident they witnessed.
related_entities: TESSERA CORPONATION Aegis CorpSec Hardened Security BCI

physical_description.visual_profile: Heavy-duty industrial apron with a commanding presence — split bib design creates a squared-off chest silhouette, while leg panels hang loose and utilitarian. Cross-back harness system adds structural weight and a tactical aesthetic. Overall impression is pure function: a garment built to survive extreme environments, worn by people who work metal and fire.
physical_description.fit: Intentionally oversized through the torso for layering over thermals and padding; leg panels are deliberately loose and split for unrestricted movement during forge work. The cross-back harness distributes weight across the shoulders, preventing sagging under the apron's considerable mass.
physical_description.primary_material: Aluminized carbon-ceramic felt (bib and skirt panels); reinforced webbing harness in synthetic aramid-weave; heat-treated leather analog binding at collar; magnetic clasps on side tabs
physical_description.texture: Heavy and dimpled — the ceramic-felt surface shows visible impact craters from welding spatter and arc flash scars. Rough-textured, with a tactile sense of abuse and survival. The leather collar is deliberately aged, with visible cracks and re-oil stains. Webbing is slightly frayed at stress points.
physical_description.color_scheme: Charred graphite (primary), rust-brown accents, deep brown heat-treated leather collar. Occasional burn marks and metallic scorch discoloration across the panels create uneven patinas. The dimpled surface catches light unevenly, giving a weathered, heat-stressed appearance.
physical_description.closures: Quick-release buckles on cross-back harness (sternum-mounted); magnetic snaps on side-tab leg panels for rapid removal; no front closure — the apron is pulled on over the head
distinctive_features: Split-bib design with reinforced grommet eyelets for tool attachment
Dimpled/cratered aluminized ceramic surface showing authentic spatter damage
Cross-back harness system with quick-release emergency buckles
Magnetically-clasped side panels for rapid leg access
Crucible forge-anvil manufacturer stamp pressed into left chest
Heat-treated leather analog collar binding — visibly cracked and re-oiled
Multiple burn streaks and oxidation marks across panels
Reinforced seaming at high-stress points; visible stitching pattern
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 3 (working class) — expensive enough to signal serious industrial work, but street-adjacent manufacturing keeps it accessible to independent fabricators and foundry workers
physical_description.cultural_context: Worn by arc welders, forge technicians, and metal fabricators across the GLMZ. The apron signals hands-on technical labor, self-reliance, and someone who works with extreme heat and danger regularly. Wearing this in public reads as 'I build things' — respected in working-class and fringe communities.
physical_description.condition_typical: Intentionally weathered and scarred. Authentic wear includes spatter pitting, burn marks, oil stains from repeated re-oiling, and thread-fraying at seams. The apron improves with age and use — each scar is a story of survived heat.
